The brick ruins visible today were originally completely covered in thick slabs of polished marble, glass mosaics, and hundreds of colossal statues.
An entirely new branch of Rome's primary aqueduct network was constructed specifically to feed these baths
summary: The second largest public baths in Ancient Rome

name: The British Museum
logistics: Hours: 10:00–17:00. Cost: £105 (timed entry — reserve ~2 months ahead).
Enter Main Gates on Great Russell Street. Bounce bag drop nearby (~£26.30).
proTips: Follow Room numbers; don't try to see everything — stick to the tactical route.
history: First public national museum in the world.
route: Enter the Main Gates on Great Russell Street, go to Ground Floor

The Rosetta Stone

  • #1 atraction
  • Features the identical decree carved in three scripts: Hieroglyphic, Demotic, and Ancient Greek.
  • This specific trilingual inscription provided the foundational key for modern scholars to finally decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs.
  • Seized by British forces in 1801 after the French originally discovered it during Napoleon's Egyptian campaign.
Walk north into Rooms 6–10 (Ancient Middle East / Assyria)

Colossal Winged Bulls (Room 6)

  • Known as lamassu, these 16-ton protective deities guarded the gates of King Sargon II's palace.
  • Carved with five legs so they appear standing firm when viewed from the front, but striding forward when viewed from the side.

Assyrian Lion Hunt Reliefs (Room 10)

  • #5 must see
  • Depicts King Ashurbanipal's staged, arena-style lion hunts, intended to showcase his divine right and ability to protect his people.
  • The anatomical precision of the dying lions is widely considered a masterclass in ancient narrative art.
Walk west through Room 18 (Ancient Greece)

The Parthenon Sculptures (Elgin Marbles)

  • #2  must see
  • Created under the direction of the master sculptor Phidias between 447 and 432 BC for the Parthenon in Athens.
  • Currently the center of one of the world's most high-profile cultural repatriation disputes between the UK and Greece.
Take the West Stairs up to Level 3, enter Rooms 54–59 (Middle East / Mesopotamia)

The Standard of Ur (Room 56)

  •  A hollow, trapezoidal wooden box from 2600 BC featuring intricate mosaics of lapis lazuli, red limestone, and shell.
  •  Displays a "War" panel and a "Peace" panel, operating as an early form of sequential comic-strip narrative.

The Royal Game of Ur (Room 56)
  • A 4,500-year-old board game; it is one of the oldest known playable games in human history.
  • The exact rules were successfully reconstructed after a curator translated a supporting cuneiform tablet in the 1980s.
Walk east across Level 3 into Rooms 40–51 (Europe)

Sutton Hoo Ship Burial (Room 41)
  • #3 must see
  • An Anglo-Saxon royal burial from the early 7th century, unearthed in Suffolk in 1939 just before WWII.
  • The iron and tinned-copper helmet is extremely rare, being one of only four intact Anglo-Saxon helmets ever found.

Lewis Chessmen (Room 40)
  • Carved primarily from walrus ivory in the 12th century, likely by craftsmen in Norway.
  • Look closely at the "warders" (the equivalent of modern rooks)—several are depicted as wild berserkers aggressively biting the tops of their own shields.
Walk north on Level 3 to Room 67 (Korea)

Sarangbang (Scholar's Study)

  • Features a life-size, meticulously reconstructed traditional Korean scholar's study.
  • Constructed entirely using traditional Korean architectural joinery, meaning no nails were used in the assembly.

Joseon Dynasty Moon Jars

  • Large, spherical white porcelain jars specifically prized for their subtle, asymmetrical imperfections.
  • Represent the core neo-Confucian ideals of the Joseon period: purity, frugality, and minimalism
summary: First public national museum in the world. Rosetta Stone, Lamassu, Elgin Marbles, Standard of Ur, Sutton Hoo, Lewis Chessmen.

name: Capitoline Hill / Piazza del Campidoglio
history:
Roman Capitoline hill

  • Citadel of early Rome
  • Was the smallest of the seven hills of Rome, but politically and religiously, it was the most important
  • It was where the government operated, where triumphant generals finished their parades, and where the most sacred religious rites took place
  • Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus was here

Piazza del Campidoglio

  • By the 1530s, the area had deteriorated into a muddy mess known as "goat hill."
  • Pope Paul III commissioned Michelangelo to completely redesign the space.
  • Michelangelo turned the square 180 degrees. Instead of facing the ancient ruins behind the hill, he oriented it outward to symbolize the shift of power away from antiquity and toward papal authority.
  • He designed a stunning, intricate 12-pointed star pattern for the ground to make the square feel like the "navel of the world." The pavement wasn't actually constructed until 1940, when the government finally ordered it finished based on the original 16th-century engravings.
notes:
The statue is of Marcus Aurelius

  • Current status is a laser-measured bronze replica installed in 1981. The original dates back to around 175 AD, and is in Capitoline Museum
  • Almost all large bronze statues from antiquity were melted down during the Middle Ages for their metal. This one only survived because early Christians mistakenly thought it was a statue of Constantine, the first Christian emperor.
  • The original statue was entirely gilded in gold. You can still see faint traces of the gilding on the original today. According to a myth, when the very last flakes of gold finally fall off the statue, it will signal the Day of Judgment
summary: Citadel of early Rome, featuring a magnificent piazza entirely redesigned by Michelangelo.

name: Castel Sant'Angelo
proTips: Great view from the top
history: Commissioned in 134 AD by the Roman Emperor Hadrian as a mausoleum for himself and his family.
Held the ashes of Rome's emperors, including Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius, and Caracalla.
By 401 AD, the mausoleum was incorporated into the Aurelian Walls as a defensive outpost to protect Rome from barbarian invasions.
410 AD, during the Visigoth Sack of Rome invaders looted the imperial burial chambers and scattered the emperors' ashes

590 AD, Pope Gregory the Great saw a vision of the Archangel Michael sheathing a sword, he interpreted it as a divine omen that the plague was finally over. 
  • He renamed it Castel Sant'Angelo (Castle of the Holy Angel)
  • The bronze statue crowning the very top of the terrace today is dedicated to the event

1527 AD, mutinous mercenary army of Holy Roman Emperor Charles V breached the walls of Rome, Pope Clement VII barely survived by fleeing the Vatican through the Passetto di Borgo.

  • 800 meter fortified corridor connecting St. Peter's directly to the castle.
  • The Pope withstood the siege and was trapped inside the fortress for seven months while Rome burned.

1538 AD. Renaissance sculptor Benvenuto Cellini was imprisoned here for allegedly embezzling Vatican funds. He escape by knotting his bedsheets into a rope and lowering himself down the massive outer walls. He broke his leg upon landing and was eventually recaptured.
route: The square and bridge leading to the castle were the sites of centuries of public executions. The Papal State's most famous executioner, Mastro Titta, carried out over 500 death sentences during his 68-year career, many of them taking place right in the shadow of the fortress walls

Instead of normal stairs at the bottom, visitors ascend through the dark, cavernous core of the building via a massive, continuously spiraling brick ramp. This is the original 2nd-century passageway used by ancient Roman funeral processions to carry the imperial ashes into the center of the tomb.
Sale Papali, lavish frescoed Renaissance rooms built so the popes could wait out long sieges in total luxury.
summary: Hadrian mausoleum, castle, papal residence, prison.

Go to Level 1

Mona Lisa (Room 711)

  • #1, must see
  • Follow sights for "La Jaconde" (Mona Lisa).
  • Painted by Leonardo DaVinci, featuring the wife of a Florentine merchant (a common person in the artwork rather than royalty).
  • Wasn't famous, until it was stolen by a museum employee in 1911 who hid in a broom closet overnight. He kept it hidden 2 years, then sold it to Italian Museum (he thought it belongs in Italy)

The Coronation of Napoleon (Room 711)

  • Napoleon is putting the crown on his own head.
  • The pope is sitting nearby, useless and bored.

Liberty Leading the People (Room 713)

  • Represents the July Revolution of 1830, not the French Revolution of 1789.
  • The young boy wielding pistols beside Liberty is widely believed to have inspired the character Gavroche in Victor Hugo's Les Misérables.
Walk towards the Center Wing (Sully)

Statue of Winged Victor (Room 703)

  • #3 must see
  • Dates to the 2nd century BC.
  • Discovered in hundreds of pieces on a Greek island and meticulously reassembled.
  • Positioned dramatically at the top of the Daru staircase to simulate the prow of a ship cutting through the wind.

history:
Where Rome was founded, allegedly where Ramus an Remulus where rescued by the she-wolf

  • Amulius stole the throne of Alba from Numitor
  • Numitor's daughter Rhea Silvia, Vestal Virgin (sacred priestess) was raped, and had twins, Ramus and Remulus
  • Amulius ordered them to be thrown in the Tiber Ribver

  • Faustulus, a shepherd, found them, raised them

  • Romulus wanted to build the city on Palatine Hill, while Remus favored the Aventine Hill. During a dispute over the city boundaries, Remus mocked the low wall Romulus was building and jumped across it. In a fit of rage, Romulus killed his brother.

route:
The Forum

  • The political, religious, and economic heart of the city.
  • A massive open square surrounded by the ruins of temples and government buildings.
  • Stand in the center and look north for a stunning, foreboding view of Mount Vesuvius looming directly over the ruins.

Temple of Jupiter (The Forum - North)

  • Originally built in the 2nd century BC to honor just Jupiter
  • After Rome conquered Pompeii in 80 BC, to enforce Roman cultural and political dominance, the temple was rededicated to the "Capitoline Triad", Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva (the three supreme deities of Rome). The inner sanctuary (cella) was physically divided into three distinct alcoves to house a statue for each god
  • Built on a towering 10-foot-high platform to elevate the gods above the bustling human marketplace of the Forum. Hidden underneath this massive podium is a network of vaulted subterranean chambers (favissae). Because it was considered the most secure and sacred building in Pompeii, these dark basement rooms were used to store the city's public treasury and valuable sacrificial offerings
Temple of Apollo (The Forum - West)

Basilica (The Forum - South West)

  • City hall, Court house at the end
  • Biggest building in town

3 Civic Halls (The Forum - South)

  • public buildings. Main one is Tabularium (central), office for public archives and mail

Building of Eumachia (The Forum - South East)

  • No one know what it was for, but it’s 2nd most impressive building in the forum (basilica is #1)

Macellum (The Forum - North East)

  • Food market
  • Circle center was used for gutting and selling fish

Theaters (East of the forum)

  • Large. 2nd centry BC, Could sit 5,000. Use for Plays
  • Small. Could sit 1,500, music & speahes. Had a roof

Gladiator barracks (South of the theaters)

  • Small room pee gladiator 
  • 2 floor is where the master lived, you can see the holes in the walls for wooden beams

The Amphitheatre (East edge of the city)

  • The oldest surviving stone amphitheater in the entire Roman world (built around 80 BC).
  • Held up to 5,000 spectators for brutal gladiator fights and wild animal hunts.
  • Can see eat numbers carved in the stone

The Forum Granary (The Plaster Casts)

  • Located on the edge of the Forum, this was essentially the city's market storage.
  • It now houses the famous plaster casts of the victims. When the volcanic ash hardened around the victims, their bodies eventually decayed, leaving human-shaped voids in the rock. Archaeologists poured liquid plaster into these voids to create perfect casts of the people (and animals, including a dog) in their agonizing final moments.
  • Also houses thousands of everyday artifacts like terra cotta pots, jugs, and tables.

The Forum Baths (or Stabian Baths)

  • Public bathing was a daily social and hygienic ritual for ancient Romans.
  • Beautifully preserved stucco ceilings and terracotta details.
  • You can clearly see the hypocaust heating system, the floors and walls are hollow so slaves could pump hot air from blazing furnaces directly into the caldarium (hot bath) rooms.

House of the Faun

  • One of the largest, wealthiest, and most luxurious private mansions in Pompeii.
  • Named after the small bronze statue of a dancing faun found sitting in the center of the front courtyard pool.

Alexander Mosaic on the floor (House of the Faun)

  • Depicting Alexander the Great battling Darius of Persia
  • Replica, real one was moved to the archaeological museum in Naples.

The Lupanar (The Brothel)

  • Ancient Pompeii's most famous and popular brothel.
  • Features small, cramped rooms with hard stone beds (they would have originally had thin mattresses on them).
  • Look up at the walls: they are covered in explicit, well-preserved frescoes. Because Pompeii was a port city with sailors speaking dozens of languages, these paintings essentially served as a visual "menu" of services so customers could point to what they wanted.

Villa of the Mysteries

  • Located a short walk outside the main city gates, which means it is often gloriously uncrowded.
  • Famous for its incredibly vivid, life-sized frescoes painted in a brilliant pigment known as "Pompeian Red."
  • The wraparound paintings depict a young woman being initiated into a secret Dionysian cult (the cult of the wine god Bacchus). It is considered one of the best-preserved pieces of ancient Roman art in the world.

House of veti

  • Best maintained 
  • Vomitorium

route:
Via Sacra

  • Most important street in ancient Rome, directly connecting the most sacred religious sites to the political centers.
  • Route which victorious Roman legions marched during grand military Triumphs.

Temple of Venus and Rome

  • Built by the Emperor Hadrian.
  • Was the largest temple in ancient Rome.

Arch of Titus

  • Built after the First Jewish-Roman War.
  • If you look at the stone reliefs inside the archway, you will see Roman soldiers carrying the Menorah and other spoils from the siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD.

Basilica of Constantine and Maxentius

  • Sprawling civic hall and law court.

Temple of Romulus

  • Huge bronze doors on this round brick building are the original ancient Roman doors, and the 1,700-year-old locking mechanism still works today.

Antoninus and Faustina Temple

  • Best-preserved structure because it was eventually converted into a Catholic church.
  • At the top of the marble columns, you can see deep diagonal grooves cut into the stone. Made by scavengers in the Middle Ages who tied heavy ropes around the columns, attempting to pull them down to steal the valuable stone, but the Roman engineering held strong.

House of Vestals

  • Home to the virgin priestesses who guarded Rome's sacred eternal flame.

Temple of Divus Julius

  • Location of Julius Caesar's funeral pyre.
  • After Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE, his body was brought to the Forum. Following Marc Antony's famous speech, the crowd became so grief-stricken and enraged that they refused to let the body be carried to the traditional cremation grounds outside the city. Instead, they gathered wooden benches, tables, and surrounding debris right there in the main square to build a massive, makeshift funeral pyre.
  • In 29 BCE, Augustus built the temple directly over the ashes of that exact pyre to formally honor him as a god.

Curia Julia (Senate house)

  • One of the most prominent and intact structures in the Roman Forum.
  • Sits squarely in the northern section of the archaeological area.
  • Remains incredibly well-preserved because it was converted into a Christian church in the 7th century.
  • The doors currently attached to the building are modern replicas. Original doors are in the Basilica of San Giovanni in Laterano, moved there in 1660. Solid bronze doors date back roughly 2,000 years. Despite their staggering weight and height, the ancient Roman balancing and hinging mechanisms are so well-designed that the doors can still be pushed open by a single person today.

Septimius Severus Arch

  • Built in 203 to celebrate victory over the Parthians.
  • After the emperor died, his son Caracalla murdered his own brother Geta to secure sole power, then ordered Geta’s name chiseled off this arch.

Temple of Saturn

  • Easily recognizable by its eight iconic surviving columns at the base of the hill.
  • Also served as the Roman Republic's main treasury (Aerarium), holding vast reserves of gold and silver securely beneath its floor.
notes: Sits in the low valley directly between Palatine Hill and Capitoline Hill. Ancient Romans would walk down from their palaces on Palatine Hill, conduct their business in the Forum, and look up at the towering Temple of Jupiter on Capitoline Hill.
summary: Epicenter of ancient Roman daily life, government, and commerce.  Where the Senate, temples, and market in ancient Rome used to be found.

name: Vatican Museums & Sistine Chapel
logistics:
Vatican museum guides

  • End at the Sistine Chappel
  • Guides are a hit or miss
  • Max size is 25 people
  • After the tour, go back to the begin of the Vatican Museum, don't exit, and go at your own pace
history: Started by Pope Julius II in early 16th century, when he acquired the Laocoön and His Sons

The Pinacoteca/Art Gallery: 

  • Masterpieces from the Middle Ages to the 1800s
  • Might not be part of the tour

The Transfiguration (The Pinacoteca)

  • Raphael's final painting, died of a sudden fever at age 37 before completing it, and it was placed at the head of his bed during his funeral. 
  • Divided into two halves: the radiant, divine transfiguration of Christ floating at the top (surrounded by El, contrasting sharply with the dark, chaotic, earthly scene below where the Apostles struggle to cure a demonically possessed boy

St. Jerome (The Pinacoteca)

  • The painting is completely unfinished. It consists mostly of monochrome underpainting (ochre and umber) on a walnut panel. Because it was never completed, you can actually see Leonardo’s fingerprints in the paint and study his raw, underlying sketching process, particularly in the highly detailed, anatomical musculature of St. Jerome's neck and shoulders
  • Was lost for centuries and famously cut into pieces. According to a popular (and likely true) legend, Napoleon's uncle, Cardinal Joseph Fesch, discovered the bottom half of the panel being used as a tabletop in a Roman antique shop in the early 19th century. Years later, he remarkably found the missing top half featuring Jerome's head being used as a stool cover or wedge in a cobbler's shop. He bought both pieces and had them pinned back together; you can still clearly see the square cut-lines dividing the saint's head from his body today.

The Pinecone Courtyard/ortile della Pigna

  • Open-air space, named for the massive ancient Roman bronze pinecone at one end

Sphere Within Sphere (The Pinecone Courtyard)

  • Sculpture by Italian artist Arnaldo Pomodoro in 1990
  • Represents the fragility and complexity of the modern world
  • You can physically push the sculpture to make the massive spheres spin on their axis

The Gregorian Egyptian Museum

  • 9 rooms dedicated to ancient Egyptian artifacts, featuring intricately painted sarcophagi, mummies, and monumental statues brought to Rome during the height of the Empire.

The Chiaramonti Museum

  • Hallway lined with over a thousand ancient Roman portrait busts and statues of gods, emperors, and ordinary citizens.

Pio Clementino Museum

  • The heart of the classical sculpture collection, iconic ancient Roman and Greek

Apollo Belvedere (Pio Clementino Museum)

  • Considered the absolute pinnacle of classical aesthetic perfection for centuries. 
  • In the Octagonal Court
  • 2nd-century Roman marble copy of a Greek bronze
  • Apollo is depicted having just shot an arrow (likely slaying the serpent Python)
  • The statue profoundly influenced Renaissance artists, who studied its contrapposto stance and idealized proportions.

Laocoön and His Sons (Pio Clementino Museum)

  • Depicting the Trojan priest Laocoön and his sons being crushed by sea serpents sent by the gods to stop him from warning Troy about the wooden horse. 
  • In the Octagonal Court
  • It was unearthed in a Roman vineyard in 1506. Michelangelo rushed to the excavation site to see it pulled from the dirt. Its massive, twisting, muscular agony directly inspired how Michelangelo painted the dramatic bodies in the Sistine Chapel.

The Belvedere Torso(Pio Clementino Museum)

  • Most famous broken statue in the world
  • Depicted Hercules resting after completing his Twelve Labors
  • When the torso was unearthed in Rome during the late 1400s, it caused a sensation. Michelangelo was absolutely mesmerized by it, famously referring to himself as a "pupil of the Torso." According to legend, Pope Julius II asked Michelangelo to restore the statue by sculpting a new face, arms, and legs for it. Michelangelo outright refused, declaring that the fragment was too beautiful and anatomically perfect to be altered.

The Gallery of Tapestries

  • A corridor lined with immense Flemish tapestries woven in the 16th and 17th centuries from designs by Raphael's students, notable for their intricate detail and subtle optical illusions.

The Gallery of Maps

  • A stunning 120-meter-long corridor covered 16th-century topographical maps
  • 80% of the maps are precise and accurate

The Raphael Rooms/Stanze di Raffaello

  • Used to be private apartments of Pope Julius III

Battle of The Milvian Bridge (The Raphael Rooms)

  • Battle in 312 AD where the Roman Emperor Constantine the Great defeated his rival Maxentius
  • It is meant to overwhelm the viewer with the sheer scale of the clash.
  • Center left, Constantine is charging triumphantly forward on a majestic white horse with his spear raised. 
  • Right side, rival Maxentius (crowned, on horseback) is desperately plunging into the rushing waters of the Tiber River as his army is pushed off the crumbling bridge
  • Top center, 3 angels hovering in the sky over the battlefield, symbolizing that Constantine's victory was the will of God

The School of Athens (The Raphael Rooms)

  • Represents the triumph of human reason
  • Depicts the greatest ancient philosophers gathered together. 
  • In the center, Plato (painted with the face of Leonardo da Vinci) points up toward the heavens and ideal forms, while his student Aristotle points forward toward the physical, empirical earth. 
  • The brooding man sitting alone on the steps in stone-mason boots is Michelangelo (representing Heraclitus). Raphael added him at the last minute after sneaking a peek at Michelangelo's work on the Sistine Chapel ceiling down the hall

The Disputation of the Sacrament (The Raphael Rooms)

  • Represents faith.
  • Spans heaven and earth, showing a straight vertical line from God the Father, down to Jesus, the Holy Spirit, and finally the Eucharist on the altar below. It illustrates that while human reason (across the room) is powerful, divine truth connects the earthly and the celestial
  • Directly across from The School of Athens

The Parnassus (The Raphael Rooms)

  • Above the window
  • Celebrates literature and music
  • Centers on the god Apollo playing a stringed instrument on Mount Parnassus. He is surrounded by the nine Muses and history's greatest poets, including Homer (looking blindly upward), Dante Alighieri in profile, and Virgil.

The Sistine Chapel

  • Were cardinals elect new pope

Michelangelo's legendary ceiling frescoes, tells the story of creation (The Sistine Chapel)

  • Michaelngelo painted the massive ceiling standing up on scaffolding he designed himself, enduring severe physical strain and complaining bitterly about the physical toll it took on his body

The Creation of Adam on the ceiling (The Sistine Chapel)

  • The most powerful element of the painting is the tiny, unbridged space between God's extended index finger and Adam's limp hand. That small sliver of negative space creates an almost electric visual tension, drawing the eye instantly to the center of the composition
  • The shape of the red mantle swirling around God and the angels perfectly matches a sagittal cross section of the human brain. Hidden message, symbolizing that God's greatest gift to humanity was not just physical life, but divine intellect and reason
  • Eve is tucked safely under God's left arm, staring intensely across the gap at Adam. She's waiting in the mind of God before her own creation

Last Judgment behind the altar (The Sistine Chapel)

  • Depicts the Second Coming of Christ and the final, eternal judgment of all humanity.
  • Acts as a giant, swirling wheel, dead are resurrected at the bottom left, the saved ascend upward to heaven on the left side, and the damned are violently thrown down to hell on the right side
  • Michelangelo painted it 25 years after the ceiling. Since, Rome was sacked in 1527 and the Protestant Reformation was dividing Europe. As a result, the optimistic, intellectual beauty of the ceiling frescoes is replaced here by a darker, heavier, and far more pessimistic tone
  • Christ in the upper center, muscular physique was modeled directly on the Belvedere Torso (seen earlier in the museum)
  • Below and to the right of Christ sits St. Bartholomew, holding a knife in one hand and his own flayed skin in the other (symbolizing how he was martyred). If you look closely at the face on the drooping, empty skin, it is a self-portrait of Michelangelo. It reflects his physical exhaustion and his feeling that painting for the Popes had "skinned him alive."
  • 13.7m x 12m

Sides depicts stories of Moses and Christ, each scene on one wall mirroring and fulfilling a scene on the opposite wall

  • 12 total

The Bramante Staircase: 

  • Located right at the museum exit, this spectacular 1932 double-helix spiral staircase is designed so that those walking down never cross paths with those walking up.

Carriage Pavillion

  • Not part of the tour
  • All the carriages used by pops over the year

history: Started out as a hunting lodge created by Louis XIII, Louis XIV's father. Louis XIV came here as a boy and expanded it when he became king. Ruled for 72 years, from age 4 to 76.One of the most important monarchs in European history. First surviving child after 23 years of marriage (his mom gave him a god complex)
Louis spent half of France's GDP to create it

Hall of Mirrors

  • Proclamation of the German Empire in 1871 after Franco-Prussian War

route: Enter via entrance A.timed entry. To the left is for no tickets, to the right is group guides
Head directly to the North Ministers Wing by 09:45 for your guided tour. This completely bypasses the massive general admission security line.

10:00 - Guided Tour of the King's Private Apartment.

  • The guided tour takes you behind the public, ceremonial State Apartments to explore the intimate "small apartment" where kings like Louis XV and Louis XVI actually lived
  • The route includes narrow passages that do not exceed 80 cm (about 31.5 inches) in width
  • The Clock Room: A private space where the king ended his evenings playing games, home to a famous 18th-century astronomical clock.
  • The Corner Room: A recently restored, highly decorated workspace used by the kings.
  • Louis XVI's Private Library: An exclusive look at the king's personal collection and reading space.
  • Louis XVI's Games Room: A refined room dedicated to court entertainment.

11:30 - Hall of Mirrors

  • Tip: stepping slightly to the sides near the interior statues will give you a clear sightline down the length of the gallery and out into the garden
  • Tip2 (not for us): Walk to the end of the hall as soon as you enter for best pictures
  • Most famous room in the palace and served as a highly trafficked corridor for courtiers, a spectacular ballroom, and a reception space for the most illustrious foreign dignitaries
  • 73 meters (240 feet) long 
  • 357 individual mirrors. Big flex as mirrors were very expensive at the time (Venice had a monopoly)
  • 40 foot vaulted ceilings, 30 paintings political, economic, and military victories of Louis XIV
  • See the replica (same artist, just 15 years later) of Napoleon's coronation

11:45 - State Apartments consist of a sequence of seven rooms, each named after a Roman deity (Hercules, Abundance, Venus, Diana, Mars, Mercury, and Apollo) 

  • The Diana Room: Originally serving as a vestibule, Louis XIV converted this space into a billiards room. He was an exceptionally skilled player, and courtiers would sit on tiered seating to watch him play.
  • The Apollo Room: This served as the main throne room. The heavy silver throne that originally stood here was later melted down to finance the King's wars, but the room retains its imposing, formal atmosphere.

12:00 - Ground floor of the South Wing/Empire Rooms

  • Napoleon crossing the Alps, a must see.
12:15 - Exit the main Palace building and walk over to the Pavillon d'Orléans.
12:30 - "Light of Liberty" VR Experience.
12:45 - Use your VR ticket's skip-the-line priority to re-enter the estate perimeter. Head straight out to the gardens.

13:00 - Latona's fountain

  • Illustrates the legend of Latona, protecting her children Apollo and Diana.

13:15 - Apollo Fountain

  • Originally Swans fountain built in 1636 by Louis XIII
  • Louis XIV, self-proclaimed "sun god", extended and added Apollo on his chariot

13:30 - The Grand Canal 

  • 23 hectares, 60m in width, 1700m east-west and 1000m north-south
  • The best places to take in the full beauty and grandeur of the estate as a whole. Laid out between 1668 and 1679, Louis XIV's architect took great care over the dimensions in order to offer the perfect perspective.

13:45 - Lunch at La Flottille
  • Have sit down and Takeaway, depending on time and weather, most likely doing takeaway
  • Alternative is The Métairie Farm, food truck next door
  • Or bring something from the breakfast shop

14:30 - Right to Grand Trianon estate

  • Louis's private apartment

14:45 - Marie Antoinette's Hamlet

  • Rustic farmhouse, she regularly went there to experience the charms of country life, surrounded by her lady's companions. It became a genuine farm, managed by a farmer, whose produce supplied the kitchens of the Palace
15:00 - Train back to main entrance
